questions.prompt: Define displacement.
questions.answer: The straight-line distance from the starting point to the finishing point, in a stated direction.

questions.prompt: Define average speed.
questions.answer: Total distance travelled divided by the total time taken.

questions.prompt: Define instantaneous speed.
questions.answer: The speed of an object at a particular instant in time.

questions.prompt: Define velocity.
questions.answer: The rate of change of displacement (displacement per unit time).

questions.prompt: Define acceleration.
questions.answer: The rate of change of velocity.

questions.prompt: State the difference between speed and velocity.
questions.answer: Speed is a scalar (magnitude only); velocity is a vector (magnitude and direction).

questions.prompt: State what the gradient of a displacement-time graph represents.
questions.answer: Velocity.

questions.prompt: State what the gradient of a velocity-time graph represents.
questions.answer: Acceleration.

questions.prompt: State what the area under a velocity-time graph represents.
questions.answer: Displacement.

questions.prompt: State what the area under an acceleration-time graph represents.
questions.answer: Change in velocity.

questions.prompt: State how a stationary object and an object moving at constant velocity appear on a displacement-time graph.
questions.answer: Stationary: a horizontal line. Constant velocity: a straight line with a constant gradient.

questions.prompt: State how constant acceleration appears on a velocity-time graph.
questions.answer: A straight line.

title: Equations of motion and free fall

questions.prompt: State the four equations of motion for constant acceleration in a straight line.
questions.answer: v = u + at; s = ½(u + v)t; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as.

questions.prompt: State the condition for using the equations of motion.
questions.answer: The acceleration must be constant (uniform) and the motion must be in a straight line.

questions.prompt: State the equation of motion that does not contain displacement.
questions.answer: v = u + at.

questions.prompt: State the equation of motion that does not contain time.
questions.answer: v² = u² + 2as.

questions.prompt: State the value of the acceleration of free fall near the Earth's surface.
Define free fall.
questions.answer: Motion under gravity alone, with no other forces such as air resistance acting.

questions.prompt: State whether the acceleration of free fall depends on the mass of the falling object.
questions.answer: No; in the absence of air resistance all objects have the same acceleration.

title: Determining the acceleration of free fall

questions.prompt: State the apparatus used to determine g with the trapdoor and electromagnet method.
questions.answer: An electromagnet, a steel ball, a trapdoor switch, a timer and a metre rule.

questions.prompt: State the measurements needed to find g using the trapdoor and electromagnet method.
questions.answer: The height h fallen by the ball and the time t taken to fall.

questions.prompt: State the equation used to calculate g from the height h and time t for a ball released from rest.
questions.answer: g = 2h/t².

questions.prompt: State one advantage of using light gates rather than a stopwatch when determining g.
questions.answer: Light gates remove the effect of the experimenter's reaction time.

questions.prompt: State two precautions that improve the accuracy of a determination of g.
questions.answer: Repeat the measurement and average; use a small dense ball to reduce air resistance; measure the height to the same point on the ball; release the ball from rest; shield the apparatus from draughts.

questions.prompt: State how g is calculated from the speeds u and v measured at two light gates a distance s apart.
questions.answer: Use a = (v² − u²)/2s.

questions.prompt: Define thinking distance.
questions.answer: The distance travelled by a vehicle during the driver's reaction time.

questions.prompt: Define braking distance.
questions.answer: The distance travelled by a vehicle while the brakes are applied and it decelerates to rest.

questions.prompt: Define stopping distance.
questions.answer: Thinking distance plus braking distance.

questions.prompt: State how thinking distance depends on speed for a constant reaction time.
questions.answer: It is directly proportional to speed.

questions.prompt: State two factors that affect braking distance.
questions.answer: Speed, road surface, tyre condition, brake condition, mass of the vehicle or weather conditions.

questions.prompt: State how braking distance changes if the speed of a vehicle doubles, assuming a constant braking force.
questions.answer: It becomes four times as large.

questions.prompt: State two factors that can increase a driver's reaction time.
questions.answer: Alcohol, tiredness, distraction, drugs or age.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by the independence of the horizontal and vertical motion of a projectile.
questions.answer: The horizontal and vertical motions do not affect each other and can be treated separately.

questions.prompt: State the horizontal acceleration of a projectile when air resistance is negligible.
questions.answer: Zero.

questions.prompt: State the vertical acceleration of a projectile.
questions.answer: g downwards (9.81 m s⁻²).

questions.prompt: State how the horizontal velocity of a projectile changes during its flight when air resistance is negligible.
questions.answer: It remains constant.

questions.prompt: State the vertical velocity of a projectile at its highest point.
questions.answer: Zero.

questions.prompt: State the shape of the path of a projectile when air resistance is negligible.
questions.answer: A parabola.

questions.prompt: Explain why a ball dropped from rest and a ball projected horizontally from the same height land at the same time.
questions.answer: Both have zero initial vertical velocity and the same vertical acceleration g, so their vertical motions are identical.

questions.prompt: State two pieces of apparatus used to investigate the motion of objects in the laboratory.
questions.answer: Light gates, a data logger, a ticker timer or a video camera.

questions.prompt: State how light gates and a data logger can be used to find the acceleration of a trolley.
questions.answer: Two light gates measure the trolley's speed at two positions a known distance apart; the acceleration is the change in speed divided by the time taken between the gates.

questions.prompt: State how the collision between two trolleys can be investigated experimentally.
questions.answer: Measure the masses of the trolleys and use light gates or a ticker timer to find their velocities before and after the collision, then compare total momentum.

questions.prompt: State the equation relating resultant force, mass and acceleration.
questions.answer: F = ma.

questions.prompt: Define the newton.
questions.answer: The force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻² in the direction of the force.

questions.prompt: State the newton in terms of S.I. base units.
questions.answer: kg m s⁻².

questions.prompt: State the direction of the acceleration caused by a resultant force.
questions.answer: In the same direction as the resultant force.

questions.prompt: State why a constant resultant force produces a constant acceleration.
questions.answer: F = ma, so with constant force and constant mass the acceleration is constant.

questions.prompt: State how the equations of motion are applied to two-dimensional motion under a constant force.
questions.answer: Resolve the force and motion into two perpendicular directions and apply the equations independently in each direction.

questions.prompt: Define the weight of an object.
questions.answer: The gravitational force acting on the object.

questions.prompt: State the equation for weight and state what g represents.
questions.answer: W = mg, where g is the gravitational field strength (force per unit mass).

questions.prompt: State the difference between mass and weight.
questions.answer: Mass is a scalar measure of the amount of matter (kg); weight is a vector force (N) due to gravity.

questions.prompt: State the S.I. unit of gravitational field strength.
questions.answer: N kg⁻¹ (or m s⁻²).

title: Tension, normal contact force, upthrust, friction and free-body diagrams

questions.prompt: Define tension.
questions.answer: The pulling force transmitted through a string, wire or rod when it is stretched.

questions.prompt: Define the normal contact force.
questions.answer: The force exerted by a surface on an object, acting perpendicular to the surface.

questions.prompt: Define upthrust.
questions.answer: The upward force on an object in a fluid caused by the difference in pressure between its lower and upper surfaces.

questions.prompt: Define friction.
questions.answer: The force that opposes the relative motion (or attempted motion) of two surfaces in contact.

questions.prompt: State what a free-body diagram shows.
questions.answer: All the forces acting on a single object, drawn as arrows showing direction and relative magnitude.

questions.prompt: Define drag.
questions.answer: The frictional force experienced by an object moving through a fluid, acting opposite to its motion.

questions.prompt: State two factors that affect the drag on an object moving through air.
questions.answer: Its speed, cross-sectional area, shape, surface texture, or the density of the air.

questions.prompt: State how the drag on an object changes as its speed through a fluid increases.
questions.answer: The drag increases.

questions.prompt: Define terminal velocity.
questions.answer: The constant velocity reached by a falling object when the drag equals its weight, so the resultant force is zero.

questions.prompt: Explain why the acceleration of an object falling through a fluid decreases as it speeds up.
questions.answer: Drag increases with speed, so the resultant force (weight minus drag) decreases and the acceleration decreases.

questions.prompt: Describe the shape of the velocity-time graph for an object falling from rest in a fluid.
questions.answer: The gradient starts steep and decreases, and the graph becomes horizontal at the terminal velocity.

questions.prompt: Describe how the terminal velocity of a ball bearing falling in oil can be determined.
questions.answer: Mark two levels on the tube, measure the distance between them, and time the ball bearing falling between them with a stopwatch or light gates; terminal velocity = distance ÷ time.

questions.prompt: State why the upper mark is placed below the surface of the oil.
questions.answer: To allow the ball bearing to reach terminal velocity before timing begins.

questions.prompt: State how it can be checked that the ball bearing has reached terminal velocity.
questions.answer: Time it between successive equal intervals; the times are equal when the velocity is constant.

questions.prompt: State two precautions when determining terminal velocity in a fluid.
questions.answer: Use a wide tube to avoid wall effects; release the ball centrally; repeat and average; measure the distance with a ruler; keep the temperature constant.

title: Moments, couples, torque and the principle of moments

questions.prompt: Define the moment of a force.
questions.answer: The force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.

questions.prompt: State the equation for the moment of a force and state what x represents.
questions.answer: Moment = Fx, where x is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.

questions.prompt: State the S.I. unit of a moment.
questions.answer: N m (newton metre).

questions.prompt: Define a couple.
questions.answer: Two equal and opposite parallel forces whose lines of action do not coincide.

questions.prompt: State the equation for the torque of a couple and state what d represents.
questions.answer: Torque = Fd, where d is the perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the two forces.

questions.prompt: State the principle of moments.
questions.answer: For an object in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about the same point.

title: Centre of mass, centre of gravity and equilibrium

questions.prompt: Define the centre of mass of an object.
questions.answer: The point at which the whole mass of the object may be considered to act.

questions.prompt: Define the centre of gravity of an object.
questions.answer: The point at which the whole weight of the object may be considered to act.

questions.prompt: State the position of the centre of gravity of a uniform metre rule.
questions.answer: At the 50 cm mark (its midpoint).

questions.prompt: Describe how the centre of gravity of an irregular lamina can be found experimentally.
questions.answer: Suspend it freely from a point and draw a vertical plumb line; repeat from a different point; the intersection of the two lines is the centre of gravity.

questions.prompt: State the two conditions for an object to be in equilibrium.
questions.answer: The resultant force is zero and the resultant moment (torque) about any point is zero.

questions.prompt: State the condition for three coplanar forces acting on an object to be in equilibrium.
questions.answer: Their vector sum is zero, so they can be represented by the sides of a closed triangle, and their lines of action meet at a point.

questions.prompt: Define density.
questions.answer: Mass per unit volume.

questions.prompt: State the equation for density.
questions.answer: ρ = m/V.

questions.prompt: State the S.I. unit of density.
questions.answer: kg m⁻³.

questions.prompt: Define pressure.
questions.answer: The force acting normally (perpendicularly) per unit area.

questions.prompt: State the equation for pressure.
questions.answer: p = F/A.

questions.prompt: State the pascal in terms of S.I. base units.
questions.answer: kg m⁻¹ s⁻².

title: Pressure in fluids, upthrust and Archimedes' principle

questions.prompt: State the equation for the pressure due to a column of fluid.
questions.answer: p = hρg.

questions.prompt: Explain why an object submerged in a fluid experiences an upward force.
questions.answer: Pressure increases with depth, so the pressure on the lower surface is greater than on the upper surface, giving a resultant upward force.

questions.prompt: State Archimedes' principle.
questions.answer: The upthrust on an object in a fluid is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the object.

questions.prompt: State the condition for an object to float in a fluid.
questions.answer: The upthrust must equal the weight of the object.

questions.prompt: State how the upthrust on an object changes as it is lowered into a liquid.
questions.answer: It increases as more of the object becomes submerged, then stays constant once the object is fully submerged.

questions.prompt: State how the upthrust on a fully submerged object changes if it is moved deeper in the liquid.
questions.answer: It stays the same, because the volume of fluid displaced does not change.

questions.prompt: Define work done by a force.
questions.answer: The force multiplied by the displacement of the object in the direction of the force.

questions.prompt: State the equation for work done by a force acting at an angle to the displacement and state what θ represents.
questions.answer: W = Fx cos θ, where θ is the angle between the force and the displacement.

questions.prompt: Define one joule.
questions.answer: The work done when a force of 1 N moves an object 1 m in the direction of the force.

questions.prompt: State the condition for a force to do no work on an object.
questions.answer: The force is perpendicular to the displacement (cos 90° = 0).

questions.prompt: State the relationship between work done and energy transferred.
questions.answer: The work done on an object equals the energy transferred to or from it.

questions.prompt: State what happens to the work done by a constant force as the angle between the force and the displacement increases from 0° to 90°.
questions.answer: It decreases, because cos θ decreases.

title: The principle of conservation of energy

questions.prompt: State the principle of conservation of energy.
questions.answer: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred from one form to another; the total energy of a closed system remains constant.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by a closed system.
questions.answer: A system that does not exchange energy with its surroundings.

questions.prompt: Name four forms of energy.
questions.answer: Kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, nuclear or electrical energy.

questions.prompt: State the energy transfers that occur when a ball is thrown vertically upwards.
questions.answer: Kinetic energy transfers to gravitational potential energy (and some to thermal energy because of air resistance).

questions.prompt: Explain why a swinging pendulum eventually comes to rest.
questions.answer: Energy is transferred to thermal energy by friction at the pivot and by air resistance, so the total mechanical energy decreases.

questions.prompt: State the equation for the kinetic energy of an object.
questions.answer: Ek = ½mv².

questions.prompt: State the equation for the gravitational potential energy gained by an object in a uniform gravitational field.
questions.answer: Ep = mgh.

questions.prompt: Define gravitational potential energy.
questions.answer: The energy stored by an object because of its position in a gravitational field.

questions.prompt: State the assumption about the gravitational field when using Ep = mgh.
questions.answer: The field is uniform, so g is constant over the height change.

questions.prompt: State how the kinetic energy of an object changes if its speed doubles.
questions.answer: It becomes four times as large.

questions.prompt: State the energy transfer that occurs as an object falls freely.
questions.answer: Gravitational potential energy transfers to kinetic energy.

questions.prompt: Define power.
questions.answer: The rate of doing work or transferring energy.

questions.prompt: State the equation for average power.
questions.answer: P = W/t.

questions.prompt: Define the watt.
questions.answer: The power of transferring 1 joule of energy per second (1 W = 1 J s⁻¹).

questions.prompt: State the equation P = Fv and the condition under which it applies.
questions.answer: Power = force × velocity, when the force and velocity are in the same direction.

questions.prompt: State the equation for the efficiency of a mechanical system.
questions.answer: Efficiency = (useful output energy ÷ total input energy) × 100%.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by an efficiency of 20%.
questions.answer: 20% of the input energy is transferred usefully and 80% is transferred to other, unwanted forms.

questions.prompt: State why the efficiency of a machine cannot exceed 100%.
questions.answer: Energy cannot be created, so the useful output energy cannot be greater than the total input energy.

title: Hooke's law and the force constant

questions.prompt: State the difference between tensile and compressive deformation.
questions.answer: Tensile deformation is stretching (extension); compressive deformation is squashing (compression).

questions.prompt: State Hooke's law.
questions.answer: The extension of an object is directly proportional to the force applied, provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.

questions.prompt: State the equation for Hooke's law and state what x represents.
questions.answer: F = kx, where x is the extension (the change in length), not the total length.

questions.prompt: Define the force constant of a spring and state its unit.
questions.answer: The force per unit extension; its unit is N m⁻¹.

questions.prompt: State what the gradient of the straight-line section of a force-extension graph represents.
questions.answer: The force constant k.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by the limit of proportionality.
questions.answer: The point beyond which the extension is no longer directly proportional to the applied force.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by the elastic limit.
questions.answer: The maximum deformation for which the object returns to its original shape when the force is removed; beyond it, plastic deformation occurs.

questions.prompt: Describe how the force-extension characteristic of a spring can be investigated.
questions.answer: Clamp the spring vertically, hang masses from it, measure the extension with a ruler for each added mass, then plot force against extension.

questions.prompt: State the measurements needed to plot a force-extension graph for a spring.
questions.answer: The force applied (from the masses) and the corresponding extension of the spring.

questions.prompt: State one precaution that improves the accuracy of a force-extension experiment.
questions.answer: Measure the extension from the same point on the spring each time; use a set square to avoid parallax; add masses gently; repeat and average.

questions.prompt: State why the spring should not be stretched beyond its elastic limit.
questions.answer: It would be permanently deformed, so the extension would no longer be proportional to the force.

title: Stress, strain and the Young modulus

questions.prompt: Define tensile stress.
questions.answer: The force applied per unit cross-sectional area: σ = F/A.

questions.prompt: Define tensile strain.
questions.answer: The extension per unit original length: ε = Δx/x.

questions.prompt: Explain why strain has no unit.
questions.answer: It is the ratio of two lengths, so the units cancel.

questions.prompt: Define the ultimate tensile strength of a material.
questions.answer: The maximum stress the material can withstand before it breaks.

questions.prompt: Define the Young modulus and state its equation.
questions.answer: The ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain in the linear region: E = stress/strain = Fl/(AΔx).

questions.prompt: State the S.I. unit of the Young modulus.
questions.answer: The pascal (Pa), i.e. N m⁻².

questions.prompt: State the measurements needed to determine the Young modulus of a metal wire.
questions.answer: The original length of the wire, its diameter (to find the cross-sectional area), the applied force and the extension.

title: Stress-strain graphs and elastic and plastic deformation

questions.prompt: State one feature of the stress-strain graph of a brittle material.
questions.answer: It is a straight line up to fracture, with little or no plastic deformation.

questions.prompt: State one feature of the stress-strain graph of a ductile material.
questions.answer: It shows a large plastic region, with the material stretching considerably before fracture.

questions.prompt: State one feature of the stress-strain graph of a polymeric material such as rubber.
questions.answer: The curve is non-linear, it can undergo very large strains, and loading and unloading follow different paths (hysteresis).

questions.prompt: Define elastic deformation.
questions.answer: Deformation in which the object returns to its original shape and size when the force is removed.

questions.prompt: Define plastic deformation.
questions.answer: Deformation in which the object does not return to its original shape when the force is removed, leaving a permanent change.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by necking.
questions.answer: The local thinning of a ductile material under tension just before it fractures.

questions.prompt: State what the area under a force-extension graph represents.
questions.answer: The work done in stretching the object, equal to the elastic potential energy stored.

questions.prompt: State the equations for the elastic potential energy stored in a spring.
questions.answer: E = ½Fx or E = ½kx².

questions.prompt: State the condition under which E = ½kx² applies.
questions.answer: Hooke's law is obeyed (the force-extension graph is a straight line through the origin).

questions.prompt: Define elastic potential energy.
questions.answer: The energy stored in an object when it is stretched or compressed.

questions.prompt: State how the elastic potential energy stored in a spring changes if its extension doubles.
questions.answer: It becomes four times as large.

title: Newton's three laws of motion
topic: Newton's laws of motion and momentum

questions.prompt: State Newton's first law of motion.
questions.answer: An object remains at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force.

questions.prompt: State Newton's second law of motion in terms of momentum.
questions.answer: The resultant force on an object is equal to the rate of change of its momentum: F = Δp/Δt.

questions.prompt: State Newton's third law of motion.
questions.answer: If object A exerts a force on object B, then object B exerts an equal and opposite force on object A.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by inertia.
questions.answer: The resistance of an object to a change in its motion.

questions.prompt: Explain why the forces in a Newton's third law pair do not cancel out.
questions.answer: They act on two different objects, so each object experiences only one of the pair.

questions.prompt: State the condition under which F = ma is a special case of Newton's second law.
questions.answer: The mass of the object is constant.

title: Momentum and impulse
topic: Newton's laws of motion and momentum

questions.prompt: Define linear momentum.
questions.answer: The product of an object's mass and velocity: p = mv.

questions.prompt: State the S.I. unit of momentum.
questions.answer: kg m s⁻¹ (or N s).

questions.prompt: State Newton's second law in the form F = Δp/Δt.
questions.answer: The resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum.

questions.prompt: Define the impulse of a force.
questions.answer: The force multiplied by the time for which it acts; it equals the change in momentum.

questions.prompt: State what the area under a force-time graph represents.
questions.answer: The impulse, which equals the change in momentum.

questions.prompt: State two ways of reducing the force experienced by an object in a collision.
questions.answer: Increase the time of the collision (e.g. using a crumple zone or airbag) or reduce the change in momentum.

title: Conservation of momentum
topic: Newton's laws of motion and momentum

questions.prompt: State the principle of conservation of momentum.
questions.answer: The total momentum of a system before a collision or interaction equals the total momentum after it, provided no external resultant force acts.

questions.prompt: State the condition for momentum to be conserved in a collision.
questions.answer: No external resultant force acts on the system.

questions.prompt: State the direction of the momentum of an object.
questions.answer: In the same direction as its velocity.

questions.prompt: State how the conservation of momentum is applied to a collision in one dimension.
questions.answer: Choose a positive direction, then equate the total momentum before the collision to the total momentum after it.

questions.prompt: State how the conservation of momentum is applied to a collision in two dimensions.
questions.answer: Resolve the momenta into two perpendicular directions and conserve momentum independently in each direction.

title: Elastic and inelastic collisions
topic: Newton's laws of motion and momentum

questions.prompt: Define a perfectly elastic collision.
questions.answer: A collision in which both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.

questions.prompt: Define an inelastic collision.
questions.answer: A collision in which momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not conserved.

questions.prompt: State whether kinetic energy is conserved in an inelastic collision.
questions.answer: No; some kinetic energy is transferred to other forms such as thermal or sound energy.

questions.prompt: State whether momentum is conserved in an inelastic collision.
questions.answer: Yes, provided no external resultant force acts.
